description: We code, we analyze, we debug at 3 a.m. Our goal is to turn NASA's open data into a project that is useful, creative and fun to show off.
summary:
We built an interactive web game that turns NASA’s satellite map of Earth’s land cover — the Near Real-Time NDVI visualization (SVS 5544) — into a soundscape generated in real time from its frames. Snow, green vegetation and dry bare ground shift across the continents with the seasons, and each of these states has its own voice. Players listen to these changes, compare the sound of different periods in a short interactive game, and only then see the image. Through the Bell, they can send nature their own signal and hear the Earth answer, feeling a resonance with it. This makes Earth observation data accessible without sight: blind and low-vision people can engage directly with the changes of our planet and control the whole interface from the keyboard.
This matters because everyone should be able to feel nature and their place within it, whatever their abilities.
details:
What it does:
The Earth Information Jukebox is a web game that turns NASA satellite data on Earth’s vegetation into sound and asks you to listen before you look. It uses the NASA SVS visualization Near Real-Time NDVI (SVS 5544, VIIRS on Suomi NPP, December 2023 – June 2026). Players hear the seasons change across Whole Earth, North America, Europe or Asia — winter snow, spring thaw, summer green, autumn decline — and only then does the image become clear.

How it works:
A Python pipeline (OpenCV) reads every frame of the NASA video, maps pixel colours to the NDVI colour bar and calculates the share of snow, bare ground and green land, mean NDVI and the speed of greening. A rule-based composer turns these values into a deterministic score that Tone.js plays in real time, in sync with the video. Snow becomes a blizzard, melting snow becomes dripping water, green land becomes wind chimes and birdsong, autumn becomes dry wind and wooden clicks, and a warm flute rises in spring and falls in autumn. The harmony moves from D minor in winter to F major in summer.
Six glowing “neurons” stand for six months, 180 days apart. Between each pair a question appears, such as “Where is nature asleep?”. The player listens to both months and chooses; the answer is computed from the data of the chosen region. A right answer connects the neurons, plays the transition between them and reveals the NASA video for that period. The Bell, the human voice in this world, lets anyone press Space so nature answers on its own.

Benefits and impact:
Blind and low-vision people can play the whole game with sound and the keyboard alone, guided by the Bell and screen-reader announcements. Everyone else learns to hear patterns in data before seeing them, which makes the experience more active and memorable. Natural sounds create an emotional connection to seasonal change, and the pipeline can be reused for other EIC visualizations and regions.

Creativity:
We reversed the usual order of perception: sound first, image second. Connecting neurons on screen mirrors the connections a person makes while listening. Most importantly, we do not set the human apart from nature: we make them part of it. Players merge with the soundscape, listen closely to its changes, witness them unfold, and through the Bell call out to nature and receive its answer. The person is no longer an outside observer of the data but a voice within the same living system.

Factors we considered:

Factors we considered
Balance between data and musicality (pentatonic scale, steady rhythm, thresholds with hysteresis); honesty about the data (we kept only regions where seasons are clearly audible and present the work as an artistic sonification, not a measurement); accessibility: blind and low-vision people can play the entire game without sight, using only the keyboard and their hearing, with keys chosen so they don’t clash with screen readers, plus spoken time periods, screen-reader announcements, no time pressure, no penalty for mistakes and a sound mixer; and licensing (all recordings credited, all other sounds synthesised, MIT-licensed code).

Tools:
Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS; OpenCV, NumPy, pandas; FastAPI; Tone.js (Web Audio API); three.js; ARIA live regions and the Web Speech API; Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages; Visual Studio Code. Developed on the team’s laptops and desktop computers.
